segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I make known to you, brothers and sisters, the good news that I announced to you, which you also received, in which you also stand,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through which you are also being saved, if you hold fast to the very terms in which I announced it to you—unless you believed in vain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After that he appeared to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After that he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Last of all, as though to a miscarried child, he appeared also to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am the least of the apostles, not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But by God's grace I am what I am, and his grace toward me did not prove empty; on the contrary, I labored harder than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So whether it was I or they, this is what we proclaim and this is what you believed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if Christ is proclaimed as having been raised from the dead, how can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then neither has Christ been raised;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation is empty, and your faith is empty too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are also found to be false witnesses about God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if in fact the dead are not raised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If it is only in this life that we have hoped in Christ, we are more to be pitied than all people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority and power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The last enemy to be abolished is death,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “he has subjected all things under his feet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when it says that all things have been subjected, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Otherwise, what will those people do who are baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they baptized on their behalf?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And why are we ourselves in danger every hour?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every day I die—I swear it by my boasting in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus on merely human terms, what do I gain? If the dead are not raised,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be deceived: “Bad company corrupts good character.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Sober up as you rightly should, and stop sinning; for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to shame you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But someone will say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fool! What you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of something else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God gives it a body just as he wished, and to each of the seeds its own body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one flesh of humans, another flesh of livestock, another flesh of birds, and another of fish.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and that of the earthly of another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; indeed, star differs from star in glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it is with the resurrection of the dead. It is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So also it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The first human, Adam, became a living being.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the spiritual is not first; rather the natural, and then the spiritual.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The first human was from the earth, made of dust; the second human is from heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As was the one made of dust, so also are those made of dust; and as is the heavenly one, so also are those who are heavenly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And just as we have borne the image of the one made of dust, we will also bear the image of the heavenly one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I am saying, brothers and sisters, is this: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, I am telling you a mystery: we will not all fall asleep, but we will all be changed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in a moment, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when this perishable body has put on imperishability and this mortal body has put on immortality, then the word that is written will come to pass:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Where, death, is your victory? Where, death, is your sting?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my beloved brothers and sisters, be steadfast, immovable, always overflowing in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not empty in the Lord.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. 'Brothers' alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are meant. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' and explain it in a footnote.

The Greek noun was an everyday word for good news, often the public announcement of a victory or a ruler's accession, and the verb beside it ('announced') comes from the same root. 'Gospel' has become a purely religious term in English and hides that ordinary sense. Both renderings are common in modern translations.

notes.traditional: first of all / as of first importance
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'among the first things', which can mean first in importance or first in time (the first things Paul taught at Corinth). Most interpreters take it as importance. 'Handed on' and 'received' are the standard terms for passing on a fixed tradition, and verses 3–5 are widely regarded as a summary formula older than the letter itself.

notes.traditional: one untimely born / one born out of due time
notes.note: The Greek word means a miscarriage or stillbirth, and in the Septuagint it is an image of something wretched and lifeless. The traditional rendering softens it and suggests only that Paul came late. Why Paul uses so harsh a word of himself is debated; it may be a term of abuse used by his opponents, or a picture of his unfitness as a former persecutor.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used for a city's citizen assembly and in the Greek Old Testament for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

In Israel's law the first portion of the harvest was offered to God, and it stood for the whole crop still to come. Paul's point is that Christ's resurrection is not an isolated event but the beginning and guarantee of the general resurrection.

The Greek word means arrival or presence. It was regularly used for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, and a first-century reader would probably have heard that association when it was applied to Christ.

The verb means to make something inoperative, to strip it of force or bring it to an end; it is not the usual word for destroying. 'Abolish' fits both the powers of this verse and death in verse 26, where the same verb recurs. Many translations use 'destroy' in both places.

notes.phrase: baptized on behalf of the dead
notes.note: The plain sense of the Greek is that some people were undergoing baptism on behalf of people who had died, and most scholars read it that way, though nothing more is known of the practice. Many other explanations have been proposed, such as baptism 'because of' the witness of dead believers. Paul refers to the practice as an argument without commending or condemning it.

The verb is the term for fighting animals in the arena. Most scholars take it figuratively, of violent human opposition in Ephesus, since a Roman citizen would not normally be sent to the beasts and Paul survived; a literal reading is possible but less likely. The words that close the verse quote Isaiah 22:13.

This is a line of Greek verse, usually attributed to the comic playwright Menander, which had probably become a common proverb. Paul quotes it as a saying his readers would recognise, not as Scripture.

The Greek adjective is formed from psychē, the word rendered 'living being' in the quotation in verse 45 (traditionally 'living soul'), so it describes a body animated by ordinary life as Adam's was. 'Spiritual' correspondingly describes a body animated by the Spirit, not one made of something immaterial. Some translations use 'physical' here, which most scholars think misleadingly suggests a contrast between material and non-material.

Many early and important manuscripts read 'let us also bear', an exhortation, which differs by a single letter in Greek. The edition translated here reads the future, as do most English versions, because it suits the argument of the passage. The choice is disputed among textual scholars.

candidates.reason: Occurs across the whole New Testament with the verb εὐαγγελίζομαι; 'gospel' versus 'good news' must be settled once so the noun and verb stay linked.
The plural as an address to mixed communities occurs in nearly every letter, and translators divide between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters'.
A favourite Pauline verb rendered variously as destroy, abolish, nullify, or do away with; readers cannot see it is one word unless the rendering is fixed by sense.
Recurs in 1 Corinthians 2:14, James 3:15 and Jude 19 in contrast with 'spiritual', and translations vary between natural, physical, unspiritual, and worldly.
Used across Paul, the Gospels and Revelation for a secret now disclosed; 'mystery' suggests a puzzle in modern English, and a single decision between 'mystery' and 'secret' is needed.
